issues.legal_issue: An eviction application is not liable to be rejected solely because material particulars of the landlord’s requirement were omitted initially when they were later supplied and the parties had a fair opportunity to address them.
material_facts: The landlord’s original eviction application did not set out all material particulars of its requirement.
The landlord supplied the necessary particulars in its rejoinder, and the tenant had notice of them.
The Rent Controller framed an issue on the landlord’s requirement, and both sides understood the case and led evidence on it.
issues.conclusion: The omission of material particulars from the original application did not justify rejecting the landlord’s claim.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 4 of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Rules is directory, not mandatory; the Court relied on M/s. Rubber House v. M/s. Excelsior Needle Industries Pvt. Ltd. (1989) 2 SCC 413.

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord pursued eviction of a tenant from rented premises.
predicates.particulars_later_supplied: The landlord later supplied material particulars of the requirement omitted from the initial application.
predicates.parties_addressed_requirement: The parties had notice of the requirement and addressed it through an issue and evidence.

issues.definition: When a landlord pursuing eviction later supplies the omitted particulars and both sides address the requirement, the claim is not rejected solely for the initial omission.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory revisional court may examine factual findings when assessing the legality or propriety of an order, but should not routinely substitute its view for that of the last fact-finding court.
material_facts: The Appellate Authority decided the landlord’s revision against the tenant in the landlord’s favour.
The tenant argued that the High Court had exceeded its jurisdiction by interfering with factual findings.
The governing rent statute empowered the High Court to examine the legality or propriety of orders and pass an appropriate order.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had not been shown to exceed its revisional jurisdiction by interfering with the Appellate Authority’s factual findings in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(6) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973 gives the High Court revisional power wider than the power under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, including power to examine factual findings. That power is not to be used routinely; interference may be justified where the last fact-finding court’s conclusion is perverse or unsupported by the material. The Court rejected the tenant’s challenge to the High Court’s exercise of that power.

predicates.landlord_revision_proceeding: A landlord pursued revision of an order in a tenant-eviction proceeding.
predicates.revisional_court_reviewed_order_legality: The revisional court examined whether the challenged order was legal or proper.
predicates.factual_finding_was_open_to_review: The factual finding was subject to review because it was perverse or could not be supported by the material before the fact-finding court.

issues.definition: In a landlord’s revision concerning eviction, a revisional court may interfere with a factual finding when it reviews the order’s legality or propriety and the finding is open to review.

issues.legal_issue: A restriction on repeated eviction for a landlord’s own use applies at the stage of deciding whether to order actual eviction, including when possession of other premises is obtained after the eviction application was filed, and is not limited to separate buildings or premises.
material_facts: While the eviction application was pending, the landlord obtained possession of three other rented premises through eviction proceedings.

The landlord maintained that possession obtained after filing the current application could not bar the current eviction and relied on High Court decisions distinguishing parts of the same premises from independent buildings.
The Supreme Court concluded that limiting the restriction to the filing stage would allow a landlord to evade it by filing multiple applications simultaneously.
The Court rejected the distinction between premises occupied by different tenants in the same building and premises in separate buildings.
issues.conclusion: The restriction extends through the stage at which actual eviction is considered, and the distinction drawn by the cited High Court decisions was not correct law; whether the other premises were of the same class remained to be determined on evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 13(1) and 13(3)(i)(b) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973 restrict the grounds and circumstances in which a tenant may be evicted. Reading the statute as a whole and in light of its purpose, the words concerning applying again cannot be confined to the filing of an application where that would defeat the restriction. The Court rejected the interpretation in Shri Brij Lal Puri v. Smt. Muni Tandon alias Urmala (1979) 1 Rent Law Reporter 58 and Jagir Singh v. Jagdish Pal Sagar (1980) 1 RLR 494.

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant for the landlord’s own use.
predicates.landlord_obtained_other_premises_under_s: The landlord obtained possession of other rented premises through proceedings on the same eviction ground, whether before or after filing the current application.
predicates.other_premises_are_of_same_class: The other premises belong to the same class as the premises for which eviction is sought.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeking eviction for its own use has obtained other premises through the same eviction ground, and those premises are of the same class, the restriction applies when actual eviction is considered.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot apply the restriction on repeated eviction without deciding whether the other premises are of the same class, and a lack of an issue and evidence on that question may require a limited remand.
material_facts: The tenant had pleaded that the landlord obtained possession of three other rented premises, and the landlord admitted obtaining possession while explaining its purposes for those premises.
No issue was framed on whether the other premises and the premises in the current application belonged to the same class.
The parties did not lead evidence on the nature or class of the premises, and deciding the question without that evidence could prejudice the landlord.
The case had already undergone a remand and had been pending for many years.
issues.conclusion: The Court remitted the case to the Rent Controller to allow evidence and decide the limited question whether the landlord had obtained possession of other premises of the same class so as to be disentitled to possession of the premises in issue.
issues.legal_principle: Application of the restriction in Section 13(3)(i)(b) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973 depends on a factual finding that the premises already obtained and the premises sought are of the same class. Where the issue was not framed and evidence was not led, the Court may remit the matter for that limited determination.

predicates.tenant_eviction_proceeding: A landlord pursued eviction of a tenant from rented premises.
predicates.prior_possession_of_other_premises_plead: The tenant pleaded that the landlord had obtained possession of other premises.
predicates.same_class_question_unresolved_for_lack_: No issue was framed and no evidence was led to determine whether the other premises were of the same class as the premises at issue.

issues.definition: When a tenant’s eviction proceeding raises the landlord’s possession of other premises but the same-class question remains unresolved for lack of evidence, the case is remanded for evidence and a decision limited to that question.
